summary:
Sri Lanka criminalises same-sex activity under Sections 365 and 365A of the Penal Code, with penalties of up to ten years' imprisonment. Section 365 addresses "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and was applied to men; Section 365A, covering "gross indecency", was amended in 1995 to reach women as well, and Outright International records both provisions as applying to men and women. Where an offence under these sections is committed by a person over 18 against a person under 16, the aggravated penalty rises to 10 to 20 years' rigorous imprisonment.

Formal prosecutions are limited. The Canada Immigration and Refugee Board's January 2012 country research recorded no convictions under the articles, yet the provisions structure everyday policing. The US State Department's country report documents police harassment of LGBT persons alongside the penal-code provisions, and Outright International reports that harassment, violence, extortion, arbitrary arrests and denial of services remain frequent.

The Sri Lanka Police are identified as the foremost perpetrators of human-rights violations against LGBTI individuals in an International Commission of Jurists opinion piece of August 2023, which notes that both the Police and the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka acknowledged this in recent months. Advocacy groups report that police routinely ignore complaints from LGBTQ victims, particularly involving sexual violence or blackmail, citing Article 365 as justification, and human rights organisations have documented police using the threat of arrest to assault, harass and extort LGBTQIA individuals.

Authorities use forced anal and vaginal examinations to seek evidence of same-sex conduct, a practice widely condemned as torture. Sri Lanka has no comprehensive anti-discrimination protections covering sexual orientation or gender identity.

Legal gender recognition is available through a certification process. The Ministry of Health issued a circular in June 2016 to health services and education institutions on issuing gender recognition certificates to transgender people, following a March 2015 complaint facilitated by the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka. No surgical intervention is legally required, but the bureaucratic certification is described as potentially onerous to obtain. The recognised identity card issued under that circular materially affects how a transgender person is treated in custody.

As of October 2024 the Prisons Department has no dedicated transgender housing. A Commissioner, Gamini Dissanayake, stated that current facilities make giving transgender prisoners their own space impossible and that separate accommodation is only planned for prisons built in future. Placement is decided case by case: trans detainees holding the recognised identity card are accommodated in line with their preferred gender where possible, while those without it undergo a doctor's assessment of whether they can be considered transgender before placement, with the inmate's preference feeding the decision. Placement by birth sex therefore remains the practical default under the existing male and female ward system, operating through a medicalised, discretionary exception process with no statutory placement rule. Officials cited concern about people accused of sex offences identifying as transgender to enter female housing as a stated reason for resisting gender-based placement.

Gender-affirming surgery is relatively inaccessible because many hospitals lack the specialised surgical units and staff required. A physician interviewed for Human Rights Watch's 2016 report stated that Sri Lankan doctors were often unfamiliar with surgical treatments for transgender patients, and patients report meeting ignorance, curiosity and ridicule from medical staff when seeking gender-confirming care, which leads some to avoid public hospitals and clinics and raises treatment costs. Obtaining hormone therapy is described as similarly fraught.

Sri Lankan family law does not recognise same-sex marriages, same-sex civil unions or equal rights for same-sex live-in couples; the marriage law dates from colonial times and is based on European law. The Catholic Church in Sri Lanka does not recognise same-sex marriages, with Cardinal Malcolm Ranjith stating that such marriages "are not a human right". A 2023 report found 69% of the population opposed to legalising same-sex unions, with 60% strongly opposed.

A bill to ban conversion therapy was tabled in March 2022 by opposition MP Rohini Kumari Wijerathna, which she said the government had failed to support as of July 2024. Despite professional college ethics, doctors are reportedly still regularly sought by families to administer such "treatment" to LGBTQ family members.

The UK Home Office's country information and policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity or expression for Sri Lanka (version 6.0, September 2024) assesses risk from state and non-state actors, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims. A joint stakeholder submission to Sri Lanka's third Universal Periodic Review cycle, filed by EQUAL GROUND with Northwestern CIHR and the GIHR, documents the criminalisation and violations reported by the NGO coalition.
tangentialFactors:
Societal attitudes are more permissive than the penal code suggests. Sri Lankan society is described as generally tolerant of homosexuality, politicians from both major parties have expressed support for LGBTQ rights, and the influential Asgiriya Buddhist chapter backs extension of rights and a constitutional amendment. In March 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa stated that he was determined to secure everybody's right to live with dignity regardless of sexuality and gender, which the Financial Times called the first such public acknowledgement by a South Asian head of state.

Survey data points the same direction. A 2021 Social Scientists Association poll found 72.5% believed LGBT people should not be punished for their sexual identity, 65% said an LGBT person can do a job as well as anyone else, and 51.4% would support rights legislation; a 2018 Equality Fund survey found 12% of respondents were LGBTQI. A separate 2023 report recorded 69% opposition to legalising same-sex unions, with 60% strongly opposed.

In August 2021 a video of a homophobic counsellor caused controversy, after which the College of Psychiatrists clarified that modern medicine does not consider homosexuality an illness and called for decriminalisation, noting that counsellors are not regulated and do not require degrees.

The National Blood Transfusion Service bars men who have anal sex with men from donating blood, classifying male same-sex intercourse as "risky behaviour" alongside drug use and having multiple partners.
localsOnly:
Community organisations include Companions on a Journey, founded in 1994 as Sri Lanka's first LGBTQ support group, the Women's Support Group (1999) and Equal Ground. Article 365 remains cited to justify police harassment and moral policing of LGBTQ people in public and private settings, which shapes how local complaints are handled.

The Committee for Protecting Rights of Prisoners has asked that future prisons give transgender and non-binary inmates a separate, chosen space, including possible space within prison hospitals, arguing that developed countries have recognised transgender rights. That advocacy, and the Commissioner's October 2024 statements, are the current reference points for the absence of a codified prison placement policy.

Accessing the gender recognition certificate depends on the June 2016 Ministry of Health circular rather than statute, and the certificate in turn governs custody placement and identity documents. Residents report that the certification process is bureaucratic even though surgery is not required.

Families continue to seek out doctors to administer conversion-style "treatment" to LGBTQ members despite the ethics positions of the professional colleges, and the 2022 bill to ban the practice remained unsupported by the government as of July 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Sri Lanka was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); its documentation of the criminalisation of same-sex activity is therefore referenced but not verified in this pass.

No entry, visa or border-screening findings specific to transgender travellers appear in the source inventory, so this record makes no assertion about immigration checks, passport markers or airport treatment.

Several care-access, marriage and public-opinion claims rest on encyclopaedic coverage rather than primary documentation, including the description of surgical capacity, the hormone-therapy account and the 2023 opposition figures; they are carried as sourced but not independently corroborated.

No youth-specific care-access findings appear in the source text, and the inventory does not resolve whether the forced examination practice has been curtailed since the condemnations recorded.

The blood-donation restriction is framed around male same-sex contact; whether it is applied to transgender donors on the basis of identity or of reported behaviour is unresolved in the sources.
